title: The Battle of Badr
teaser: 313 men. 2 horses. 70 camels. Against an army of 1,000. And Allah called it 'The Day of Criterion.'

layers.title: The Numbers
layers.subtitle: What the two armies looked like
layers.content:
The Muslim army that marched to Badr was made up of 300-317 men — 82-86 Emigrants and the remainder from the Aws and Khazraj. They were not well-equipped: only two horses, 70 camels shared between multiple men. The Prophet ﷺ, Ali ibn Abi Talib, and Marthad bin Abi Marthad shared a single camel between three.

The Quraysh army numbered approximately 1,000 — with 700 camels and 300 horses. They had brought with them singers and musicians, intending to make the victory a celebration. The leaders of Quraysh had come personally.

The Prophet ﷺ made du'a before the battle with such intensity that Abu Bakr came to him and said: 'O Messenger of Allah, your Lord will fulfil His promise to you.' Allah then revealed: 'Allah has already made you victorious at Badr when you were a weak little force.' (3:123)
layers.quran_ref: Quran 3:123 — 'Allah has already made you victorious at Badr when you were a weak little force'
layers.source: Safiur-Rahman Al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar (Ar-Raheeq Al-Makhtum), Darussalam

layers.title: The Night Before
layers.subtitle: The Prophet's du'a and Allah's promise
layers.content:
The night before the battle, the Prophet ﷺ prayed and made du'a until dawn. He said: 'O Allah, if this group is destroyed today, You will not be worshipped on earth.' He raised his hands until his cloak fell from his shoulders. Abu Bakr picked it up and placed it back, saying: 'O Messenger of Allah, your Lord will fulfil His promise to you.'

Allah sent down sleep upon the Muslims as a mercy and security. He sent rain that night — it firmed the sandy ground for the Muslims but made the Quraysh's ground soft and difficult. And then He sent the angels.

The Quran records: 'When you were calling upon your Lord for help, and He responded: I will reinforce you with a thousand angels, following one after another.' (8:9)
layers.quran_ref: Quran 8:9 — 'I will reinforce you with a thousand angels following one after another'
layers.hadith_ref: The Prophet's du'a before Badr — Sahih Muslim
layers.source: Safiur-Rahman Al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar (Ar-Raheeq Al-Makhtum), Darussalam

layers.title: The Battle
layers.subtitle: 73 minutes that changed Arabia
layers.content:
The battle began with individual duels. Utbah bin Rabi'ah, his son Al-Walid, and his brother Shaybah stepped out from the Quraysh lines. Hamzah, Ali, and Ubaydah bin Al-Harith stepped out for the Muslims. All three of the Quraysh were killed.

Abu Jahl — the man who had tortured Sumayyah, who had placed a stone on Bilal's chest, who had called the Prophet a liar — was killed that day by two young men from the Ansar: Muadh and Muawwidh, sons of Afra. When Ibn Masud found him still alive and finished him, he brought his head to the Prophet ﷺ.

The Quraysh army broke. Seventy of their number were killed. Seventy were taken prisoner. Among those killed were the greatest enemies of Islam — Umayya bin Khalaf (Bilal's torturer), Utbah, Shaybah, and Abu Jahl.

Allah called this day Yawm Al-Furqan — The Day of Criterion — because it separated truth from falsehood forever.
layers.quran_ref: Quran 8:41 — 'And know that whatever you obtain of war booty, then indeed for Allah is one fifth of it'
layers.hadith_ref: Account of the Battle of Badr — Al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar
layers.source: Safiur-Rahman Al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar (Ar-Raheeq Al-Makhtum), Darussalam

layers.title: After the Victory
layers.subtitle: What the Prophet ﷺ did with the prisoners
layers.content:
The prisoners of Badr presented the Prophet ﷺ with a decision. Umar ibn al-Khattab said: kill them. Abu Bakr said: ransom them and use the wealth for the Muslims.

The Prophet ﷺ chose ransom. For those who could not pay, an alternative was offered: teach ten Muslim children to read and write and go free. Education in exchange for freedom.

Abu Jahl's head was brought to the Prophet ﷺ. He looked at it and said: 'This is the Pharaoh of this ummah.'

The Prophet ﷺ stood over the mass grave of the Quraysh dead and called each of them by name: 'O Utbah bin Rabi'ah. O Shaybah bin Rabi'ah...' He said: 'We have found what our Lord promised us to be true. Have you found what your Lord promised you to be true?' Umar said: 'O Messenger of Allah, do you speak to people who are dead?' He replied: 'They hear me no less than you do — but they cannot answer.'
layers.quran_ref: Quran 8:67 — 'It is not for a prophet to have prisoners of war until he has thoroughly subdued the land'
layers.source: Safiur-Rahman Al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar (Ar-Raheeq Al-Makhtum), Darussalam

layers.title: The Legacy
layers.subtitle: What Badr established
layers.content:
Badr established four things that would define Islam's trajectory:

First — the principle that truth does not guarantee safety, only ultimate victory. The 313 were not powerful. They were right. And rightness, sustained by Allah's support, overcame power.

Second — the People of Badr became a category in Islam. The Prophet ﷺ said of the Companions of Badr: 'Perhaps Allah has looked at the people of Badr and said: Do as you please, for I have forgiven you.' They held a station no one else would ever hold.

Third — the Day of Criterion separated Madinah's political reality from Makkah's. Before Badr, the tribes of Arabia waited to see which side would win. After Badr, the answer was clear.

Fourth — the treatment of prisoners at Badr set a precedent for Islamic ethics in warfare: prisoners have rights, ransom is legitimate, and knowledge is worth more than wealth.
layers.quran_ref: Quran 8:8 — 'That Allah might establish the truth and abolish falsehood, even if the criminals disliked it'
layers.hadith_ref: The Prophet ﷺ said: 'Perhaps Allah has looked at the people of Badr and said: Do as you please, for I have forgiven you.' — Sahih Al-Bukhari
layers.source: Safiur-Rahman Al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar (Ar-Raheeq Al-Makhtum), Darussalam

quiz.prompt: What were the numbers at Badr?

options.text: 100 Muslims vs 500 Quraysh
313 Muslims vs approximately 1,000 Quraysh
500 Muslims vs 700 Quraysh
200 Muslims vs 900 Quraysh

quiz.scholar_reflection: 313 men, 2 horses, 70 camels — against 1,000 with 300 horses and 700 camels. Allah called this day a victory and named it Yawm Al-Furqan.

quiz.prompt: What alternative to ransom did the Prophet ﷺ offer illiterate prisoners at Badr?

options.text: Physical labour for one year
Teaching ten Muslim children to read and write
Converting to Islam
Military service for the Muslim army

quiz.scholar_reflection: Education in exchange for freedom. The Prophet ﷺ valued knowledge so highly that it was made equivalent to ransom.

quiz.prompt: What did the Prophet ﷺ say when he stood over the grave of the Quraysh dead and called to them?

options.text: May Allah have mercy on those who repented before their death
We have found what our Lord promised us to be true — have you found what your Lord promised you to be true?
Your enmity to Islam is now finished'),('d','O enemies of Allah, you refused guidance

quiz.scholar_reflection: He spoke to the dead. When Umar questioned this, he replied: they hear me no less than you do — but they cannot answer.

quiz.prompt: Who killed Abu Jahl at Badr?

options.text: Hamzah ibn Abd al-Muttalib
Ali ibn Abi Talib
Two young men from the Ansar — Muadh and Muawwidh sons of Afra
Bilal ibn Rabah

quiz.scholar_reflection: Two young men who had been tormented — and the community that had been tormented — watched the man who ordered Sumayyah's death fall at Badr.

quiz.prompt: What did Allah call the Battle of Badr?

options.text: Yawm Al-Nasr — The Day of Victory
Yawm Al-Furqan — The Day of Criterion
Yawm Al-Iman — The Day of Faith
Yawm Al-Qadar — The Day of Power

quiz.scholar_reflection: Al-Furqan means that which separates truth from falsehood. Allah named this battle the separator. Not the victory — the criterion.

quiz.prompt: The Muslim army at Badr was outnumbered 3:1, with almost no horses and shared camels. They won. What does this teach you about the relationship between means and outcomes in Allah's plan?

options.text: Means matter — the Muslims prepared and fought; they were not passive
Outcomes are ultimately determined by Allah, not the balance of forces
The weakness of the means made the victory more clearly Allah's
All of these — preparation and tawakkul are not opposites

quiz.citation: Quran 3:123 — 'Allah has already made you victorious at Badr when you were a weak little force'
quiz.scholar_reflection: They prepared. They marched. They fought. And Allah sent angels. Both are true simultaneously — human effort and divine support are not alternatives.

quiz.prompt: The Prophet ﷺ prayed before Badr until his cloak fell from his shoulders. Abu Bakr gently replaced it. What does this scene tell you about du'a and about the relationship between them?

options.text: The intensity of the Prophet's du'a shows how much this moment mattered even to him
Abu Bakr's gesture was itself a form of support — physical care as an act of faith
Du'a is not passive — it is the most active thing a believer can do in a crisis
All of these are visible in this one moment

quiz.citation: Account before Battle of Badr — Al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar
quiz.scholar_reflection: He prayed until he was physically exhausted. This is what du'a looks like when the stakes are absolute.

quiz.prompt: Abu Jahl — who had tortured the weak, killed Sumayyah, mocked the Prophet ﷺ for thirteen years — was killed by two young men of the Ansar. What do you feel when you reflect on that?

options.text: Relief that Allah's justice is real and operates in this world
Soberness — what happened to him can happen to anyone who persists in oppression
The weight of how long the believers endured before this day
All of these at the same time

quiz.citation: Account of Abu Jahl's death at Badr — Al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar
quiz.scholar_reflection: He was not killed by a general or a hero. He was killed by two young men from Madinah who had heard his name their whole lives. That is its own statement.

quiz.prompt: The People of Badr were told: do as you please, for I have forgiven you. What does a station like this — earned through one act of sacrifice — tell you about how Allah values singular moments of commitment?

options.text: One decision, made with complete sincerity, can define a person's standing forever
The people of Badr were ordinary people who showed up — their station came from showing up
Allah does not measure lives only by their length but by their moments
All of these — the station of Badr is an argument against feeling it is too late

quiz.citation: Sahih Al-Bukhari — the Prophet's words about the People of Badr
quiz.scholar_reflection: They marched out not knowing they would win. They marched out not knowing this day would define their eternal standing. They just showed up.

quiz.prompt: The Prophet ﷺ chose to ransom prisoners rather than execute them. Abu Bakr supported this; Umar disagreed. Then a verse came criticising the choice, yet the Prophet's mercy was not condemned — only the premature choice of ransom before fully establishing power. What does this nuanced divine response teach you about mercy and justice?

options.text: Both mercy and justice are from Allah — neither cancels the other
Timing matters in applying each — what is right depends on what stage you are at
Even the Prophet ﷺ's instincts toward mercy were not always perfectly timed
All of these — the Quran's nuanced response is itself a teaching

quiz.scholar_reflection: Allah did not say the mercy was wrong. He said the timing was premature. There is a difference between a principle being right and its application being wise.
